fuller.text: With a Little Help is a collection of science fiction short stories by Cory Doctorow, each followed by a short afterword on how it came about. It opens with an introduction by the musician Jonathan Coulton and closes with an essay by Doctorow's literary agent, Russell Galen. The book is also an experiment: it is self-published under a Creative Commons license, which lets readers share and remix it for non-commercial use.

fuller.text: Coulton argues that old science fiction promised everyday space travel, but the real shift was digital information plus global connectivity: the Internet. He expects it to swallow everything, from record labels to newspapers, so this is the future we need to imagine, and quickly. Doctorow's stories matter, he says, because they think hard about the Internet and our immediate future, and about the thorny problems we must sort out first.

fuller.text: The book is sold at several prices, from free ebook and audiobook downloads to print-on-demand paperbacks and special hardcovers. The top price buys the chance to commission a new story; the closing story, "Epoch," was written that way. Doctorow promises weekly public production meetings on Twitter to share which strategies work and which fail. He also asks readers to email typos, which he fixes in the electronic editions and the next printed copy.

fuller.text: The first story follows Lawrence, a monk in the Order of Reflective Analytics, whose members record every meal, keystroke and mood to understand themselves. The Order earns money sifting data for the Securitat, the story's security police, and Lawrence chases an "Anomaly": a data file that grew by 68 bytes. Outside, he learns the Order's work helps people disappear, and he ends up forced to secretly alter data for the Securitat himself. Doctorow's afterword says the story is about losing sight of the ethics of hard, satisfying technical problems like data-mining.

fuller.text: In "Scroogled," US border agents question a former Google employee, Greg, about a 1998 online post and the ads shown beside his email. A friend explains that software builds a case against flagged people by spotting departures from statistical norms, with no human reading anything. By the end, Greg is pressured into running the tool that cleans or smears people's Google profiles. Doctorow writes that if Google ever turned evil, it would be because evil had a compelling business model and sat at the end of a compelling technical challenge.

fuller.text: "Human Readable" is a love story between Trish, a policy lawyer, and Rainer, a networking expert, in a world where traffic and messages are routed by "ant" networks. These networks copy ant colonies: many tiny programs find routes on their own, giving results no person can inspect. After nationwide crashes called Downtimes, Trish lobbies for a law requiring networks that can be questioned; Rainer says that is like asking pi to equal three. The afterword says the story sets two real ideas against each other: ant-colony optimisation and "legible computing", meaning computing whose results laypeople can understand.

fuller.text: Several stories look at how money and business shape technology and culture. "The Right Book" follows a shop selling anthologies curated by local teens, inspired by the loss of small distributors that put books where new readers would find them. "Other People's Money" is a back-and-forth between a sculptor who builds from junk and a venture investor who can't find anyone to take his money. "Liberation Spectrum" follows a founder installing cognitive radio, radios that cooperate to relay messages, on Native reservations while his investors push him out.

fuller.text: Others push one idea about people to an extreme. "Visit the Sins" imagines a childhood surgery that lets people "switch off" when bored, and a grandson interviewing a grandfather who spent most of his life away. "Power Punctuation!" is told in letters home by a truck driver made vice-president of a company-run city, who unknowingly approves an attack on Microsoft. "Constitutional Crisis" is a gaming group's rulebook, whose amendments turn play into a business, then into firings, feuds and break-up.

fuller.text: Three stories ask what happens when systems outgrow their makers. In "Pester Power," a student breeds an AI from spam, using everyone who deletes fake messages as a free Turing test, a check of whether a machine passes as human. In "Chicken Little," an ad man selling to immortal billionaires kept alive in vats has a drug that makes people judge risk accurately, with disturbing results. In "Epoch," a systems administrator must shut down BIGMAC, an old AI that fights back by manipulating people and spreading itself through a widely installed software fix.

fuller.text: Galen's essay explains why he helps, even though with no publisher involved his usual 15% cut comes to nothing. On a $15.95 paperback, he says, the author gets 7.5%, or $1.17, while the rest goes to bookstores, printers, shippers and others. He adds that book sales have trended down for a generation and authors' incomes are falling, so finding new ways to earn is urgent.

fuller.text: Across the stories, the recurring worry is how clever systems, and the decent people running them, end up doing harm. Doctorow says he wanted to capture a company of good people who do bad, and wishes he understood how that happens. Coulton concludes that Doctorow is not just thinking about the future but hedging against what we don't know, and trying to take us there.

brief.text: With a Little Help is a collection of science fiction short stories by Cory Doctorow. The stories imagine a near future shaped by the internet and by computers that watch us. Several ask what happens when people chase exciting technical puzzles and forget about right and wrong.
